sections.overview: The arrow cichlid, called mojarra flecha in Spanish, is a cichlid found only in Nicaragua’s volcanic Lake Apoyo. It is one member of the lake’s endemic Midas-cichlid flock.
sections.identification: Its slim, arrow-shaped body, narrow tail stalk and silvery-grey sides distinguish it from deeper-bodied, bottom-oriented Amphilophus in the lake. Seven dark flank blotches form a broken stripe and fuse into bars during breeding, when both sexes darken. FishBase lists 20 cm total length. Breeding residents averaged 23.6 ± 0.5 cm for males and 20.1 ± 0.4 cm for females; length type is unstated and the difference was not significant (p = 0.06). No reliable adult height, width or mass range was found.
sections.habitat: It is adapted to open water rather than the bottom, swimming away from shore and the benthic zone more often than its high-bodied lake relatives.
sections.diet: Stomach-content analyses found winged insects in every sampled arrow cichlid, while both it and the bottom-feeding Midas cichlid consumed biofilm. It is partly piscivorous, but detailed prey proportions remain sparse.
sections.behavior: Breeding adults establish and defend fixed territories, usually caring for broods together around the nesting site.
sections.reproduction: Parents guard young, and biparental care continues for about a month after fry begin swimming freely.
sections.ecology: Its elongated shape is linked to open-water swimming, unlike the compact, high-bodied benthic species living alongside it. The Lake Apoyo Midas cichlids are studied as an example of ecological diversification within one isolated lake.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered (CR), assessed in 2019. Its entire known range is Lake Apoyo, with an estimated extent of occurrence and area of occupancy no greater than 22 km²; invasive fishes threaten habitat and young native fish.
